steps: Agree the teams joining after the pilot with your administrators and governance owner, then set the organization-wide access setting, user and group overrides and a Coworker user group per team.
Map the roles each group holds in your connected applications, and agree which task types must use Plan mode, who approves them and which actions each sandbox allows, deletes included.
Write the rules for adding servers and installing or removing plugins, the memory rules, the audit review routine, joiner and leaver steps and an AI credit plan.
Test with users from each group that they reach only what their application roles allow, and bring the policy to your administrators and governance owner for approval.
deliverables: Access model with user groups and overrides
Action and approval rules by application and sandbox
Server, plugin, memory and audit rules
AI credit plan, and joiner and leaver steps
asks: A Coworker administrator, a System Admin or a Product Admin of Experience Platform, to apply the settings
A governance owner to agree the action rules and approve the policy
Any governance and approval workflows Adobe's onboarding team has defined, so we build on them
risk: Changes to your data that no one checked first: we agree which tasks must use Plan mode, where Coworker waits for approval, and which actions each sandbox allows.
outcome: Your agreed teams use Coworker under an approved policy, with access set by group, agreed actions and approvals in each application and sandbox, and an AI credit plan.

steps: Agree with your system owner and security team the tools the server offers, read-only by default, and which write tools must ask for confirmation before they act.
Build and host the MCP server in a location you own, with the authentication method and headers Coworker sends and a tool timeout that suits your system.
Register it in Coworker as a server, over SSE or HTTP at its URL, and test each tool with authorized and unauthorized users.
Hand over the code, the tool list with its read and write scope, the run and removal instructions and a record of who may add servers.
deliverables: MCP server code and hosting setup
Tool list with read and write scope
asks: Your system's API documentation, a test environment and credentials
A hosting location you own for the server
Your security owner to review the integration and approve the server
risk: A tool that changes your system without a check: tools are read-only by default, write tools ask for confirmation, and we test that unauthorized requests are refused.
outcome: Authorized users complete the agreed tasks in your system through Coworker, on a server your security owner has approved, and unauthorized requests are refused.

steps: Choose the use cases for your usage-bound Coworker trial with your business owners, and agree a success measure and a credit budget for each one.
Prepare the data access and example prompts for each use case, checking that each pilot user acts only within their existing product permissions.
Run the use cases with your pilot users within the Coworker trial's AI credits, tracking use on the license usage dashboard and logging example results.
Report the time saved, the quality of results and the open issues against each success measure, with recommendations for your purchase decision.
deliverables: Use case briefs with success measures
Credit budget for each use case
asks: Business owners to choose the use cases and agree how success is measured
Pilot users with time to run the use cases
An administrator who can view AI credit usage on the license usage dashboard
risk: Using up the Coworker trial's AI credits before every use case is tested: we set a credit budget for each use case and track use on the license usage dashboard.
outcome: Your sponsor has a value report showing each use case's measured result against its success measure, to decide on a purchase from results in your own environment.

steps: Run Coworker's implementation guide skill with your team for the agreed path, answering its discovery questions about your environment, licensing and planned data ingestion.
Check each planned step against your live tenant's licenses, sandboxes, schemas, datasets, report suites and permissions, and correct the owners and effort where they differ.
Import the checked plan into Workfront or Jira, and agree with your project owner the owner and the delivering service for every step.
deliverables: Checked plan with owners, effort and dependencies
List of steps the tenant check changed
Plan imported into Workfront or Jira
asks: People with access to your tenant's licenses, sandboxes, schemas, datasets, report suites and permissions
A project owner to approve the plan and name each step's owner
A choice of Workfront or Jira for the delivery plan
risk: A plan that does not match what your tenant really holds: the skill does not read your systems, so we check every step against the live tenant before approval.
outcome: Your project owner approves a delivery plan in Workfront or Jira, checked against your live tenant, where every step names an owner and the service that delivers it.

steps: Once your upgrade steps are complete, agree with your analytics owner the report suite and data view pairs to validate and the matching rate each must reach.
Run Coworker's validation skill on each pair, a single metric or dimension or a full audit of up to 40 metrics and 20 dimensions, and check each suggested action.
Fix the causes in Experience Platform, Adobe Analytics or the data view, such as bot filtering, session settings, marketing channel derived fields or duplicate datasets, and rerun.
Document the differences that are expected by design, such as device-based visitors against people, and record your analytics owner's sign-off for relying on CJA.
deliverables: Sign-off record for relying on CJA
asks: Users who can view both the report suite and the data view
An analytics owner to agree the matching rate and sign off the results
risk: Chasing every last difference when some variance is expected: we fix real causes and document the differences that come from design, such as device-based visitors against people.
outcome: Each agreed pair reaches the agreed matching rate, or every remaining gap is explained and accepted, so your teams can rely on CJA data.

steps: Coach an analyst from your team as the Coworker champion, and agree with them the approved dimensions, metrics and segments in each team's data view.
Tidy the names and descriptions of those components in CJA so prompts can name them exactly, and write a library of vetted prompts built on them.
Write one Skill that directs Coworker to the approved components, test it against the prompt library, and store each team's data view in Coworker's memory.
Teach your users when to ask Coworker for a quick answer and when to work through a deeper analysis, using your own prompts and data.
deliverables: Approved component list for each data view
Memory preferences and a short user guide
asks: An analyst to act as your Coworker champion and approve the library and Skill
View access for your users to the agreed data views
An administrator to set up your organization's skill library, so the Skill reaches every team
risk: Answers built from the wrong or unapproved components: the Skill directs Coworker to your approved components, and each team's data view is stored in memory.
outcome: Your pilot users get answers built from your approved components for every prompt in the vetted library, with a Skill and library your champion has approved.

steps: Start from the Streaming Media plan Coworker's implementation guide skill produced, and agree with your video team the player platforms and media events to collect.
Configure the datastream and the XDM schema and dataset for media events, then implement the SDK or API in each agreed player and map the media event model.
Add the media components to your CJA data view where CJA reports, so your analysts can use the new media data.
Run test sessions on each platform and check that starts, pings and completions reach your CJA or Adobe Analytics reports, recording the evidence.
deliverables: Player implementation on each agreed platform
Media event mapping and data view components
asks: Developer access to your player code on each agreed platform
A video team contact to agree the events and check the test sessions
Your Streaming Media plan from Coworker's implementation guide skill, if you already have one
risk: Media data that never reaches reporting: we run test sessions on each platform and check starts, pings and completions in your reports before sign-off.
outcome: Your media players on the agreed platforms send Streaming Media data on the Edge, and test sessions show starts, pings and completions in your CJA or Adobe Analytics reports.

steps: Add MCP Read-only Access to your pilot users' Adobe Analytics product profiles, or MCP Full Access where they may also create segments, calculated metrics or projects.
Check that the aa-mcp integration is connected in Coworker, agree the report suite each team uses, and store it as a preference in Coworker's memory.
Write starter prompts, including root cause questions about a known metric over a known period, and compare the first answers with the same reports in Analysis Workspace.
Write and test one Skill that keeps Coworker on your approved components, and give your pilot users a short guide.
asks: A system or product administrator to add MCP permission items to product profiles
Your pilot users and the report suite each team uses
The reports your teams trust today, to compare the first answers against
risk: Answers that differ from the reports your teams already trust: we compare the first answers with Analysis Workspace, and a Skill keeps Coworker on your approved components.
outcome: Your pilot users ask Coworker about your Adobe Analytics report suites in plain language, within their own permissions, and its answers match Analysis Workspace for the agreed reports.

steps: Review the latest health check results for the agreed sandboxes in Coworker with your platform owner, and agree which failed checks to fix.
Let Coworker fix the issue types it supports after you approve each change: identity namespace descriptions, duplicate and default merge policy names, and schemas missing the audit field group.
Fix the other failed checks by hand, such as schema and identity configuration, TTL and lookback settings, destination schedules, scheduled queries and source credentials.
Add descriptions to the XDM fields your teams target on, confirm the fixes on the next daily scan, and hand over a prioritized list of open issues with owners.
deliverables: Health check results before and after
Prioritized list of open issues with owners
asks: Users with permission to view health checks and the Experience Platform permissions each fix needs
A platform owner to approve each change and the remaining list
A development sandbox to try changes to identity linking or merge behavior first
risk: A fix that changes how profiles link or merge in production: we try those changes in a development sandbox first, and you approve every change before it is made.
outcome: The agreed failed health checks pass on the next daily scan, and your platform owner has a prioritized list of what is left, each item with an owner.

steps: Use Coworker's Data Management Agent to list the large, unused or forgotten Experience Event datasets in the agreed sandboxes, and agree a shortlist with your data owners.
Check how actively each shortlisted dataset is used, and model the effect of a retention period on it, by row count and storage size.
Review each dataset with its owner against your business and legal retention needs, and choose another data lifecycle tool where a whole dataset must go.
Apply the approved retention policies after reviewing Coworker's impact preview, and record each one with its audit log entry and the owner's sign-off.
deliverables: Dataset shortlist with usage and impact evidence
Retention decisions signed by the data owners
Applied policies with their audit log entries
asks: Data owners who can decide retention for each shortlisted dataset
Access to the Data Management Agent, and permissions for the datasets and retention actions
Your business and legal retention requirements for event data
risk: Removing data a team still needs: usage signals may not cover every factor, so each data owner signs every decision before a policy is applied.
outcome: Each approved retention policy shows in its dataset's settings and audit log, and your data owners have signed every decision behind it.

steps: Each month, run Coworker's Data Validation skill on your agreed critical datasets and their key identity and event fields, and check streaming capacity and breaches for each sandbox.
Follow up flagged values with Query Service where a sample is not enough, and log each regression with its cause in the monthly data quality log.
Agree fixes to mappings or source data with your data owners, check fixed fields on the next run, and review the volume with you after three months.
deliverables: Monthly data quality log by dataset and field
asks: The critical datasets and their key identity and event fields to check
Data owners who agree fixes and their dates each month
Your change control process for fixes to mappings and source data
risk: A regression missed because the skill reads only a sample: where a sample is not enough, we supplement its results with Query Service checks.
outcome: Each month your agreed critical datasets are checked, every regression has an owner and a fix date, and fixed fields pass on the next run.

steps: Give your practitioners the Manage Journeys, View Journey Events, Data Sources and Actions, View Segments and Manage Segments permissions, and keep other users read-only.
Check that your audiences, events and data sources exist, name your custom actions so prompts can call them exactly, and write a prompt guide for journey requests.
Pilot journeys from prompts or flowchart images, then finish in the journey canvas what Journey Create does not set, such as A/B tests, dataset lookups and custom action field mapping.
Check every expression, run Coworker's quick simulation and then a manual simulation or test mode, and publish each journey once your journey owner approves the checklist.
deliverables: Role setup record and readiness checklist
asks: Configured journey events, data sources and custom actions, with your audiences already created
A journey owner to approve the pre-publish checklist
Journey requests from your team to pilot, as prompts or flowcharts
risk: A journey published with the wrong fields or values: we check every expression Coworker creates, and a quick simulation never replaces a manual simulation or test mode.
outcome: Your practitioners build journeys from prompts or flowcharts with Coworker, finish them in the journey canvas, and publish only after the agreed simulation and test cases pass.

steps: Run Coworker's journey hygiene, custom action error and channel configuration checks on the agreed sandbox, and agree with your Journey Optimizer owner what to clean up.
Rename journeys, actions and events with missing, generic or similar names, close old live journeys to new entrances, and delete the stale drafts and finished journeys you no longer need.
Move the journeys that stay into folders with tags, split oversized journeys, and fix the endpoints, authentication or payloads behind failing custom actions.
Correct sender, reply-to, subdomain, IP pool and unsubscribe settings in Journey Optimizer, since Channel Operation only reads them, then rerun the checks to confirm the fixes.
deliverables: Hygiene and channel findings before and after
Naming rules for journeys, actions and events
asks: Users with journey view and manage permissions and access to your channel configurations
A Journey Optimizer owner to decide what to keep and approve the remaining list
Your approval for each change to a live journey
risk: Cutting off customers already in a journey: we close old live journeys to new entrances instead of stopping them, and live changes go through new versions you approve.
outcome: A rerun of the hygiene and channel checks shows the agreed items fixed, and your journey inventory follows agreed naming, folders and tags.

steps: Agree with your messaging team the service to connect, its HTTPS endpoint, headers and authentication method, the throttling policy, the message payload and every payload scenario you send.
Create the custom channel with Coworker's Channel Builder skill, and test each payload scenario while the channel is still a draft, checking your provider's logs.
Activate the channel, then set up its API credentials where it uses authentication, its channel configuration and, where link tracking is needed, a delegated subdomain.
Use the channel in a first journey or campaign, and check that test messages reach your provider for each agreed payload scenario.
deliverables: Active custom channel with API credentials and channel configuration
First journey or campaign using the channel
asks: Your provider's HTTPS endpoint, its API documentation and test credentials
Administrators with the View custom channels and Manage custom channels permissions
Access to your provider's logs to confirm each test request arrived
risk: A payload or endpoint error found after activation, when those fields are locked: we test every payload scenario while the channel is still a draft.
outcome: Your messaging service works as an active custom channel in Journey Optimizer, tested for each payload scenario and sending from a live journey or campaign.

steps: Check that your approved brand guidelines for voice, imagery and legal are published where the Brand Lookup skill finds them, and set up the reusable email design system Coworker maintains.
Store the Figma access token in Coworker's secrets and agree frame conventions with your designers, so Build Email from Figma builds from frames as they should ship.
Define the brand, compliance, design and accessibility (WCAG 2.1 AA) reviews each email passes, and agree how approved content is saved into your Journey Optimizer templates.
Pilot emails from brief to saved draft with your content team, and fix the template issues the reviews find before your content owner approves the guide.
asks: Your approved brand guidelines and your existing email templates and fragments
A Figma access token and designers to agree the frame conventions
A content owner to approve the guide and the pilot emails
risk: Generated content treated as ready too early: every email passes the agreed brand, compliance, design and accessibility reviews, and is reviewed before it is saved.
outcome: Your team produces emails with Coworker from brief to saved draft, each passing the agreed reviews and saved into the right Journey Optimizer template.

steps: Set up Loyalty roles with your administrator, including custom roles with Loyalty permissions in non-production sandboxes, and check that the eligible audiences exist in Experience Platform.
Configure the reward providers, event mappings, product inventory, exclusions and identity settings in Loyalty configurations, with your loyalty platform team.
Build the first challenges with Coworker's Loyalty Challenge Management skill, and write the challenge messages and content cards it does not fully automate.
Review each challenge and its generated journey with your loyalty lead before publishing, then check that test members complete the tasks and receive the reward.
deliverables: First published challenges with their messages
asks: Reward fulfillment APIs and loyalty events from your loyalty platform
An administrator to assign Loyalty roles in each sandbox
A loyalty lead to agree the first challenges and approve them before publishing
risk: Members who do not receive a reward they earned: we review each challenge and its generated journey before publishing, and check with test members that rewards arrive through your provider.
outcome: Your team builds loyalty challenges with Coworker on a configured program, and the first challenges are live with their messages and reporting in the loyalty dashboards.

steps: Run Coworker's Target program audit and Recommendations checks on your account, and agree with your Target owner which findings to fix.
Resolve collisions and priority conflicts between activities and fix misconfigured ones, agreeing each change to a live activity with its owner first.
Archive stale activities, remove the audiences and offers no activity uses, and fix the feeds, catalog attributes and criteria behind empty or stale recommendations.
Give Coworker your past test history as a CSV, so its next-test advice draws on your own learnings, then rerun the audit to confirm the fixes.
deliverables: Cleaned activity, audience and offer inventory
asks: Users with Target roles that allow the agreed changes
Activity owners to agree each change to a live activity
Your past test history from your own records, as a CSV
risk: Changing a live activity someone relies on: we agree each change to a live activity with its owner first, and rerun the audit to confirm the result.
outcome: A rerun of the audit shows the agreed findings resolved, your Target inventory is clean, and Coworker's next-test advice draws on your own test history.

steps: Run Coworker's Dispatcher Insights on your production and stage environments within its seven-day log window, sharing your Dispatcher configuration and related AEM code for review.
Add the Governance Agent's vulnerability list, and agree with your AEM owner a prioritized fix list: cache rules and headers, filters and routing, redirects, security headers and affected components.
Implement the agreed fixes in your code, including permission-sensitive caching and CSRF and CORS settings, and deploy them through Cloud Manager.
Ask Coworker to reassess the logs or live URLs after each deployment, and record before and after evidence and the items outside your control.
deliverables: Before and after evidence from Coworker
List of items outside your control
asks: Developers with Cloud Manager access to deploy and to share the Dispatcher configuration and code
An AEM owner to agree the fix list and approve the remaining items
risk: A fix that breaks caching or access on the live site: we try each change on stage first, deploy through Cloud Manager and ask Coworker to reassess afterwards.
outcome: The agreed Dispatcher, security and vulnerability fixes are live in production, and Coworker's reassessment shows the targeted issues resolved.

steps: Agree with your content owner the fragment folders and the launch they must be ready for: semantic search, translation, headless delivery or publishing.
Run Coworker's Content Fragment inspection on each folder, and work through its human-reviewed remediation steps for model, metadata, schema and reference issues.
Check dependencies before any delete, resolve the risky ones, and agree the tags and review step for Coworker's bulk fragment edits.
Rerun the checks until each folder passes, testing model changes that affect live delivery on a lower environment first.
asks: Access to the agreed Content Fragment models and folders
A content owner to approve the bulk edit rules
A lower environment to test model changes that affect live delivery
risk: Deleting a fragment that other content still uses: we check dependencies before any delete and resolve the risky ones first.
outcome: Each agreed fragment folder passes the readiness checks for your planned launch, and your team edits fragments in bulk under agreed tags and a review step.

steps: Gather your style guide, claim rules, positioning and design standards with your brand owner, and import your brand policies from PDF or page URLs.
Review the rules and checks the Governance Agent extracts, add segments such as markets, audiences or sub-brands over your global defaults, and enter your design system's colors and typography.
Map your domains, and set the brand, rules, checks and domains to Active, since new entities start as Draft and only Active ones are used.
Run a batch analysis of existing pages, report aligned and non-aligned pages, and agree with your brand owner a fix plan and owners for rule updates.
deliverables: Populated Experience Context for your brand
Batch analysis results with a fix plan
asks: Your current brand documents: style guide, claim rules, positioning and design standards
A brand owner to approve the rules and checks and own their updates
The domains and existing pages for the batch analysis
risk: Rules that look set up but never apply: new entities start as Draft, so we set each to Active and confirm the checks run on your domain.
outcome: Brand checks run on your agreed domain from an approved Experience Context, and the batch analysis of existing pages is your baseline for fixes.

steps: Find expired, expiring and undated assets in the agreed folders with the AEM Governance Agent in Coworker, and add expiry dates and usage rights metadata to them in bulk.
Set a review routine for assets about to expire with your rights owner, based on your own rights terms.
Create Content Hub access rules for your groups, regions or agencies as ALLOW rules on IMS Group IDs, with a rule for every group that must see all assets.
Apply the least-privilege group and ACL changes the Governance Agent recommends after diagnosing your repository permissions, then test with users from each group.
deliverables: Content Hub access rules with test results
asks: Your rights terms and access policy for the agreed folders
The IMS Group IDs and the groups that must see all assets
Test users from each group to check what they can see
risk: Groups locked out of Content Hub: groups no rule covers are denied access, so we add a rule for each group that must see all assets and test with users.
outcome: Agreed assets carry expiry dates and rights metadata, your groups see only the assets their rules allow in Content Hub, and permission changes pass your access review.

steps: Each month, list the failed and warning executions of the agreed scenarios with Coworker, and have it explain each error.
Check which scenarios depend on a connection, webhook or data store before changing it, then fix the failing scenarios and expired connections.
Report the month's failures, fixes and open risks, keep the record of who holds the write tools current, and review the volume with you after three months.
deliverables: Record of who holds the write tools
asks: A Fusion administrator to turn on MCP access and decide who holds the write tools
Your confirmation before any destructive change, such as a delete
Owners for failures in the systems your scenarios connect to
risk: A change that breaks other scenarios: we check which scenarios depend on a connection, webhook or data store before changing it, and destructive changes need your confirmation.
outcome: Each month your agreed Fusion scenarios are reviewed, every failure has a fix or an owner, and destructive changes happen only with your confirmation.

steps: Review Adobe's default Organizational Rules with your marketing operations owner, and agree your naming patterns for programs, emails and Smart Campaigns.
Write your required folders, tokens and reports and your compliance rules, such as unsubscribe links, footer details, UTM parameters and exclusion filters.
Set the global rules and the agreed workspace overrides, update the version number, and test the rules with Validate Programs on real programs.
Tune rules that block good programs, then send your marketing operations team a change note on what changed and why.
deliverables: Organizational Rules document with version history
asks: An administrator to edit the rules, since that needs admin permissions
Your current naming conventions and compliance standards for programs and emails
Real programs to test the rules against
risk: Rules so strict they block good programs: we test them with Validate Programs on real programs and tune any rule that fails work your team would approve.
outcome: Coworker in Marketo Engage builds, plans and validates programs against your own approved rules, with global rules, workspace overrides and a version history.

steps: Each month, take the agreed campaign briefs from your team, plan each program with Plan Campaigns and build it from the right template with Build Programs.
Finish what stays manual: Smart List filters for your real segments, Smart Campaign flow steps, the placeholder emails and any dynamic content.
Run the manual checks Coworker flags and run Validate Programs against your own rules, then fix what fails.
Activate each program once you approve it, and review the monthly volume with you after three months.
deliverables: Plan and validation result for each program
Manual check record for each program
asks: Campaign briefs, approved copy and target segments each month
Templates with at least one email and one Smart Campaign
An approver for each program before it is activated
risk: A program activated with the wrong audience or logic: filters and flow steps stay manual, so we set them by hand and validate every program before you approve it.
outcome: Each month your agreed campaign briefs become Marketo Engage programs that pass Validate Programs and the manual checks, and are activated with your approval.

steps: Run AI-decisioning health with your marketing operations owner to see persona classification and coverage across demographic, firmographic, technographic, psychographic, persona and intent data.
Define your personas from your person attributes in the persona mapping panel, so more of your people are classified into a persona.
Set the intent model's activity weights with Coworker's Intent configuration skill, activate the approved model, and check the results with Analyze intent.
Rerun AI-decisioning health, compare it with the first report, and agree an enrichment plan for the coverage gaps that remain.
deliverables: Active intent model and its weights
AI-decisioning health reports before and after
Enrichment plan for the remaining gaps
asks: A marketing operations owner to approve the personas, weights and enrichment plan
Users with the permission to view B2B intent reports
Your persona definitions as your sales and marketing teams use them today
risk: Weights that skew how people are scored: only one intent model is active and it drives the scoring, so you approve the weights before we activate them.
outcome: Persona classification improves against your first AI-decisioning health report, the approved intent model is active, and you have an enrichment plan for the remaining gaps.

steps: Create the webinar with Coworker in its program at your licensed capacity, and design the registration page and room in the Adobe Connect design surface.
Build the promotion journey Coworker drafts, then finish what it lists as left to configure: the audience, the invitation email, the registration form event filter and member status steps.
Build the post-webinar journey with its attended and no-show paths, then test registration, the joining link and the follow-up emails before publishing.
Leave a reusable webinar program with a prompt guide, so your team can run later events the same way.
deliverables: One live webinar with its promotion and follow-up journeys
Reusable webinar program with a prompt guide
asks: The webinar's content, speakers and approved emails
The audience to invite and the registration form to use
A test group to register and attend before publishing
risk: Registrants who never get the joining link or the right follow-up: we test registration and the invitation before publishing, and check both follow-up paths and the member status steps.
outcome: Your first interactive webinar runs from a tested registration path, attendees and no-shows each get the right follow-up, and your team can reuse the program.
